```{r setup, message=FALSE, echo=TRUE, collapse=TRUE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(echo = FALSE)

# load libraries
library(tidyverse)
library(here)

# load raw data
alignments <- read_tsv(here("data", "alignments.csv"))
episodes <- read_tsv(here("data", "episodes.csv"))

# set theme
theme_set(hrbrthemes::theme_ipsum_gs())
```

### The mystery

I recently stumbled across an old John Oliver episode from Season 1. The pace of that episode was *noticeably* slower — so slow in fact that I thought I had YouTube on half speed.

**My interest was piqued: has John Oliver’s speech become more fast-paced over time?**

(For what it's worth — for social media attention I {c|sh}ould have asked **"Has John become more *angry*?"** — but I'm a data scientist, not a loudmouthed journalist, so we'll leave *that* inference to someone else.)

### The short story

Yes, it has. And by *a lot*.

Over the 11 seasons in this data set, John Oliver has increased from an average of **150 words per minute to almost 180**.

For comparison: 100—120 words per minute is [generally considered](https://virtualspeech.com/blog/average-speaking-rate-words-per-minute) as "slow", 120—150 as "conversational", and from 200 and up, we're talking auctioneer-like style. A speaking rate of 160 is a threshold for "comfortable" hearing and processing of information — there is, after all, a recommendation to keep presentations to between 100 an 150 words per minute on average


![](../data/graphs/LWT_overall.png)
In case anyone's wondering: generally, starting the y-axis at anything but 0 is considered bad and deceptive practice. However, 100 is quite a natural starting point since speaking rate does not have it's natural default at 0.

**The key insights:**

* Significant increase in speaking rate over time
* During Covid - where John broadcast without an audience - the average is higher. This probably reflects the absence of interruptions by audience reactions; it otherwise continues the overall trend.
* The length of the segments over which the speaking rate was calculated *also* increases over time — it is possible that the increase in speaking rate is primarily due to artifacts in the data.

### The (slightly) longer story

**Task**: In general, dealing with questions of this type is a rather straightforward corpus linguistic task: we can measure the speaking rate in **words per minute** — simply counting the words and divide by duration of the segment. With more advanced NLP tools, we can also measure **syllables per second** and **pauses between words**.

**Challenge**: How do we deal with artifacts in the data that are unrelated to speech style? For example, just by looking at the increase of length of a segment, it could be that breaks or intro/outros are simply less influential in longer segments and thus contribute to a relative increase in speaking rate. It could also be that speech from *other* people simply became less frequently featured over time.

Let’s see.

### The data

Using [yt-dlp](https://github.com/yt-dlp/yt-dlp), I fetched the audio, the auto-generated subtitles and file meta data such as file duration from a [list of 314 episodes of Last Week Tonight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Last_Week_Tonight_with_John_Oliver_episodes) from the first 11 seasons. The data is based on the *main segments* of each episode, which range in duration from 6 to 34 minutes.

*Note: To assess if other people's contributions affected the counts, I manually checked about two dozen transcripts. They did in fact change the numbers, but in the other direction. That is, if we excluded all non-John data, his speaking rate would be even **higher**. But importantly, they did not change the overall pattern.*

#### Simple method: Episode-level

For the graph above, I used the simple methods by words per minute, such as in this table. Not all main segments are online, or subtitles and meta data is not available (the `NA` in the table):

```{r episodes_inspect, echo=TRUE, collapse=TRUE}
# subset episodes, rename columns for readability, and determine wpm speech rate
episodes_clean <- episodes |> 
  select(season, episode_total, main_segment, duration, length, wrds) |> 
  rename(Season = season,
         Episode = episode_total,
         Title = main_segment,
         Duration = duration,
         Words = wrds) |> 
  mutate(`Words per minute` = Words/(length/60))

# output table
episodes_clean |> 
  select(-length) |> 
  head(10) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 0, caption = "Episode list for the first 10 episodes in Season 1.") |> 
  kableExtra::kable_styling()
```

#### Advanced method: Word-level

If we go to the **word-level**, we can add more weight to the argument that the increased speaking rate is in fact not an artifact of text composition or other data quality issues.

For a random third subset of 108 segments, I used [Gentle](https://github.com/lowerquality/gentle) to force-align the audio file with the text. This determines the beginning and end of each word that allows us to measure the duration of each word.

Gentle works reasonably well on audio files longer than a few seconds — while it comes at the cost of accuracy, patterns should be clear enough in over 370,000 measured words.

The packacke {nsyllables} counts the syllables per word.

```{r alignments_transform, echo=TRUE, collapse=TRUE}
# adds duration, pauses, medians
alignments <- alignments |> 
  group_by(ep_id) |> 
  # normalize 
  mutate(beg = round(beg, 4),
         end = round(end, 4)) |> 
  mutate(pause = lead(beg) - end,
         dur = end - beg) |> 
  mutate(syl = nsyllable::nsyllable(word)) |> 
  mutate(sps = (1/dur)*syl) |> 
  ungroup()
```

This table illustrates this for Episode 18 in Season 8, ["Housing Discrimination"](https://youtu.be/_-0J49_9lwc?si=jkoQM6E-U-Rec9mZ):

``` {r alignments_inspect, echo=TRUE, collapse=TRUE}
# illustrate for one episode
alignments |> 
  filter(ytid == '_-0J49_9lwc') |> 
  # column names that are better to read
  rename(Date = ytdate, 
         Word = word,
         Recognised = recog,
         `No of syllables` = syl,
         Begin = beg,
         End = end,
         Duration = dur,
         `Syllables per second` = sps,
         `Pause to next word` = pause) |> 
  select(Word:End, Duration, `Pause to next word`, `No of syllables`, `Syllables per second`) |> 
  head(12) |> 
  knitr::kable(digits = 2, caption = "Forced-alignment for S08E18, 'Housing Discrimination'. ")

```

```{r alignments_summary}

# each segment's summary
alignments_summ <- alignments |> 
  # filter durations of less than 0.2 (likely alignment errors):
  filter(dur > 0.19 | is.na(dur)) |> 
  group_by(season, ep_id, ytdate, ytid) |> 
  summarize(words = n(),
            sum_na = sum(is.na(beg)),
            align_errors = sum_na/words,
            sps_mean = mean(sps, na.rm = T),
            pause_mean = mean(pause, na.rm = T),
            .groups = "drop_last") |> 
  ungroup()
```



```{r alignments_plot, fig.height = 7, fig.width = 10, message = FALSE}
alignments_summ |> 
  # exclude all where the mean of pauses in an episode is greater than 200ms
  filter(pause_mean < .20) |> 
  select(ytdate, ep_id, align_errors, pause_mean, sps_mean) |> 
  # pivot longer to make a facet plot
  pivot_longer(pause_mean:sps_mean,
               names_to = "metric",
               values_to = "value") |> 
  # change order of metrics to have syllables first in plot
  mutate(metric = factor(metric, levels = c("sps_mean", "pause_mean"))) |> 
  # change from seconds (decimal) to milliseconds
  mutate(value = if_else(metric == "pause_mean", value * 1000, value)) |>
  # scatterplot
  ggplot(aes(ytdate, value)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "#b73779") +
  facet_wrap(~metric, scale = "free_y", #nrow = 2,
             labeller = as_labeller(c(sps_mean = "Syllables per second", pause_mean = "Pause duration in milliseconds"))) +
  labs(title = "More syllables per second and shorter pauses",
       subtitle = "Additional indicators of faster speaking rate over time\nthat are independent of show segment properties",
       x = '',
       y = '',
       caption = "108 episodes with forced-alignment") +
  scale_x_date(date_breaks = '1 year', date_labels = "%Y") +
  theme(panel.grid.minor = element_blank())
```

Now combine with episode data

```{r correlate_epi-wrd, fig.height = 10, fig.width=8}
comb_dat <- episodes |> 
  select(ep_id, season, episode_total, period, ytdate, wrds, length) |> 
  left_join(alignments_summ |> select(ep_id, sps_mean, pause_mean), join_by("ep_id")) |> 
  mutate(wpm = wrds/length*60, .after = length) |> 
  filter(!is.na(ytdate)) |> 
  # episode within
  group_by(season) |> 
  mutate(ep_within = row_number()) |> 
  mutate(period = factor(period, levels = c("precovid", "covid", "post_covid"))) |> 
  ungroup()

# make model data
mod_dat <- comb_dat |>
  select(ytdate, ep_within, period, wrds, wpm, length, sps_mean) |> 
  mutate(ytdate_num = as.numeric(scale(as.numeric(ytdate))),
         length = as.numeric(scale(length)),
         ep_within = as.numeric(scale(ep_within)))

# simple linear model
mod_wpm <- lm(wpm ~ length + ep_within + period + ytdate_num, data = mod_dat)
summary(mod_wpm)

performance::model_performance(mod_wpm)
performance::check_model(mod_wpm)
performance::check_heteroscedasticity(mod_wpm)
performance::check_collinearity(mod_wpm)

```


### Predictive modelling

While by now we have a pretty good indication that John's speaking rate has in fact increased — corroborated of course by a pure auditory impression alone — we can use this data set to illustrate the advantage of linear regression. Because at face value, all we have in data terms is: "increase in words per minute" **and** "increase in amount of text", so technically, we still don't know which causes which.

In theory, we could be modelling either `words per minute` or `syllables per second` — the latter has more data, but is also vastly more complex to perform, and, if using the aggregate or average, has only about a third of the data points we have for `words per minute`. The third option, `word duration` comes with a whole other complexity of word properties that we'll leave for today.
